claims.text: The material is an equiatomic, single-crystal FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy with an FCC structure.
Yielding is initiated by Shockley partial dislocations emitted from pre-existing vacancy clusters or surface defects.
The unstable stacking-fault energy modulates the barrier for partial-dislocation nucleation.
Shockley partial dislocations on {111}<112> systems create intrinsic stacking faults on {111} planes.
Stress concentrations at vacancy clusters facilitate thermally activated passage over the unstable stacking-fault-energy barrier.
The <11-1> loading orientation has a higher maximum yield stress than the <110> orientation.
The <11-1> orientation produces a higher resolved shear-stress component on the primary {111}<112> slip system than the <110> orientation.
The higher resolved shear stress in the <11-1> orientation causes a higher applied stress to be required for partial-dislocation emission.
The <11-1> orientation will have approximately 10–15% higher yield strength than the <110> orientation.
Increasing temperature reduces the unstable stacking-fault energy and critical resolved shear stress through enhanced atomic vibrations.
Yield strength decreases monotonically with increasing temperature from 100 K to 600 K.
Dislocation density increases with strain rate because there is insufficient time for dislocation annihilation.
Yield strength is relatively insensitive to strain rate between 10^8 and 10^10 s^-1.
The HCP-like regions are transient intrinsic stacking faults rather than a true phase transformation.
The HCP-like regions lack the long-range hexagonal order expected for epsilon martensite.
The HCP-like regions lack the magnetic signature expected for epsilon martensite.
HRTEM and SAED can distinguish stacking faults from an HCP phase by detecting stacking-fault fringes and the absence of HCP diffraction reflections.
EELS can establish that the HCP-like regions have no change in Fe/Ni local magnetic moments.
Neither deformation twinning nor an FCC-to-BCC transformation occurs under the stated conditions.
Strain rates above 10^10 s^-1 may produce shock-induced amorphization.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes the higher <11-1> yield stress to a higher resolved shear-stress component or Schmid factor, but for a fixed CRSS a higher Schmid factor implies that a lower applied stress is needed to initiate slip. Thus the stated Schmid-factor premise conflicts with the claimed higher applied yield stress.

The initial state permits a defect-free crystal, while the proposed governing mechanism requires pre-existing vacancy clusters or surface defects and the structural mediator specifically assigns vacancy clusters as nucleation sites. No alternative homogeneous-nucleation mechanism is specified for the defect-free case.
